```{r setup, include = FALSE}
source("_setup.R")
library(bayesmokken)
```

```{r fits, include = FALSE}
data(srs)
fit <- bb_mokken_h(srs, draws = 2000, seed = 1)
reporting_fit <- bm_cached("srs_50000")
reporting_interval <- bm_interval(reporting_fit)
reporting_mc <- bm_mc_diagnostics(reporting_fit)
reporting_digits <- 3L
reporting_unit <- 10^(-reporting_digits)
stopifnot(
  reporting_interval$total_draws == 50000L,
  max(reporting_mc$lower_endpoint_mcse,
      reporting_mc$upper_endpoint_mcse) < 0.5 * reporting_unit
)
```

This vignette is about getting results *out* — into a table, into a sentence,
and into the reproducibility appendix a reader needs to check your work.

## What the fitted object holds

```{r anatomy}
names(fit)
```

You rarely need to reach into it directly. Every element has an accessor that
returns a plain data frame with a fixed set of columns, and those columns are
pinned by an installed schema that the test suite checks against.

| Accessor | Returns |
|---|---|
| `bm_scale_h()` | one row: the scale coefficient |
| `bm_item_h()` | one row per item |
| `bm_pair_h()` | one row per item pair |
| `bm_interval()` | the interval, its method, and its status |
| `bm_draws()` | the bootstrap draws |
| `bm_provenance()` | hashes, seed, versions |
| `bm_diagnostics()` | denominator, regularity, transport, Monte Carlo |
| `bm_report()` | a formatted table |

```{r accessors}
bm_scale_h(fit)
str(bm_draws(fit, what = "scale"), give.head = FALSE)
```

For the broom ecosystem, `tidy()` and `glance()` are also available:

```{r broom}
generics::tidy(fit)
generics::glance(fit)
```

## Tables

`bm_report()` renders in three forms. A data frame, when you want to keep
working with it:

```{r report-df}
bm_report(fit, what = "scale", format = "data.frame")
```

Markdown, to paste into a Quarto or R Markdown document:

```{r report-md}
bm_report(fit, what = "scale", format = "markdown")
```

And LaTeX:

```{r report-tex}
bm_report(fit, what = "item", format = "latex", digits = 3)
```

A `bm_report` carries the rendered table alongside the notes and the method
identifier that belong with it, so that a table cannot travel without its
provenance. The table itself is in `$table`, and it is an ordinary data frame,
so it composes with whatever table package you already use:

```{r kable}
knitr::kable(
  bm_report(fit, what = "scale", format = "data.frame")$table,
  caption = "Scalability of the eleven-item SRS."
)
```

```{r report-notes}
bm_report(fit, what = "scale", format = "data.frame")$notes
```

## Sentences

The hard part of reporting is usually prose, not tables. Three templates, each
of which says exactly what the object supports.

**Scale level.**

> The eleven-item scale had $H =$ `r fmt_h(reporting_interval$point_estimate, reporting_digits)`,
> 95% CI `r fmt_ci(reporting_interval, reporting_digits)`. The interval is a repeated-sampling
> confidence interval obtained by Bayesian bootstrap over respondents, with the
> width correction of Lee (2026) applied.

That copy-ready sentence uses `r format(reporting_interval$total_draws, big.mark = ",")`
draws. Endpoint Monte Carlo standard errors are
`r formatC(reporting_mc$lower_endpoint_mcse, format = "f", digits = 6)` and
`r formatC(reporting_mc$upper_endpoint_mcse, format = "f", digits = 6)`.
Both are below half of the `r formatC(reporting_unit, format = "f", digits = reporting_digits)`
reporting unit, which is the executable precision rule in the setup chunk.

**Item level.**

> Item coefficients ranged from
> `r fmt_h(min(bm_item_h(fit)$H))` to `r fmt_h(max(bm_item_h(fit)$H))`.
> Item-level intervals are reported without the width correction, which was
> validated for the scale coefficient only.

**Two cluster targets.**

```{r cwb, include = FALSE}
cwb_r <- bm_interval(bm_cached("cwb_respondent"))
cwb_e <- bm_interval(bm_cached("cwb_equal_cluster"))
```

> Under respondent weighting $H =$ `r fmt_h(cwb_r$point_estimate)`, 95% CI
> `r fmt_ci(cwb_r)`; under equal-cluster weighting $H =$
> `r fmt_h(cwb_e$point_estimate)`, 95% CI `r fmt_ci(cwb_e)`. The two targets
> are different population quantities and differ here because cluster size is
> informative. The respondent target corresponds to sampling a pupil
> uniformly; the equal-cluster target corresponds to sampling a classroom
> uniformly and then a pupil uniformly within it. We report the respondent
> target because the former sampling operation is our target population.

That last clause — *why* you chose the target — is the one readers cannot
reconstruct and the one most often omitted. When informative cluster size is
plausible, fit both targets, compare them, and state which population operation
the primary result represents.

### Three sentences not to write

**Do not write:** "There is a 95% probability that $H$ lies in [.104, .162]."
The interval is a repeated-sampling confidence interval. The Bayesian bootstrap
is how it is computed, not what it means, and the package deliberately reports
no probability statement about $H$ at any level.

**Do not write:** "$H$ was significantly above .30." Nothing here is a
hypothesis test. The landmarks are descriptive conventions from the Mokken
tradition, and `bm_benchmark()` will give you the arithmetic relation without
dressing it as a decision.

**Do not write:** "After removing the two weakest items, $H$ rose to .38, 95%
CI [.31, .45]." The interval does not carry across a change of item set,
because the estimand is a *declared, fixed* scale. Refitting after item
selection is a new analysis whose uncertainty does not include the selection
you just performed.

## The reproducibility appendix

```{r provenance}
bm_provenance(fit)
```

`analysis_input_hash` is the full input receipt: it includes the complete
scored response matrix, included row IDs, item order, normalized point weights,
declared supports, and clustered labels/target when applicable. The narrower
`row_hash`, `item_set_hash`, `score_map_hash`, `support_hash`, and
`cluster_id_hash` fields diagnose selection and schema differences; they are
not substitutes for a response-value hash.

Report the full hash with the seed, draw count, package version, and method ID.
Together they identify what was run. Exact stochastic recomputation also
requires the recorded RNG and execution contract; fresh independent draws are
compared through Monte Carlo error, not promised to match to the last digit.

## Citation

```{r cite}
bm_cite(fit)
```

The two methods have separate sources, and `bm_cite()` returns the ones that
apply to the fit in hand rather than a blanket list. A BibTeX form is available
with `format = "bibtex"`.

## The status of item-level intervals

This deserves its own section, because it is the single easiest thing to
over-report.

```{r item-intervals}
head(bm_item_h(fit, include_interval = TRUE), 3)
```

Item-level endpoints are honest uncorrected bootstrap quantiles. What they are
not is *calibrated*: the width correction was trained and confirmed against the
scale coefficient, and no equivalent evidence exists for item coefficients. The
`interval_calibration` column says `uncalibrated` in every row so that the
distinction survives being copied into a table.

You may report them. Say what they are when you do, and do not compare them
against the scale interval as though the two carried the same guarantee.
